title: Monotonic stack
when: "Nearest element to the left (or right) that is larger (or smaller)"
How far a value stays the maximum or minimum of a stretch
Sum or count over all stretches of their maximum or minimum
Largest rectangle under a histogram
idea:
Sweep the array once, keeping a stack of positions whose values are in decreasing order. Before pushing the current position, pop every position whose value is not larger than the current one: those can never again be "the nearest larger" for anything to the right, because the current element is nearer and at least as large. After the popping, the top of the stack is the nearest larger element to the left.

Every position is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole sweep is linear even though it has a loop inside a loop.
traps: Decide strict or non-strict on purpose: popping on "less than or equal" finds the nearest strictly larger element. For sums over all stretches use strict on one side and non-strict on the other, or equal values are counted twice.
Store positions on the stack, not values.
When nothing is left on the stack, the answer is "none": use a sentinel such as 0 or n + 1 consistently.

title: Blocks of a binary string
when: An operation acts on a whole substring of a binary string (flip it, reverse it, sort it, delete it)
"Minimum number of operations to make the string all equal, sorted, or alternating"
The answer does not seem to depend on how long the runs are
idea:
Stop looking at characters and look at the boundaries: the places where two neighbouring characters differ. Add an imaginary 0 before the string and after it. Inverting a substring changes only the two boundaries at its ends, and each of them is toggled. A string is all 0s exactly when there are no boundaries.

So with B boundaries you need at least B / 2 moves, and since each block of 1s contributes exactly two boundaries, inverting the blocks one by one achieves it. The answer is the number of blocks of 1s. Most "operate on a substring" problems fall to the same view: count what an operation can change, get a lower bound, then meet it.
traps: Count blocks by their starts: a 1 whose left neighbour is not a 1.
Remember the ends of the string: a block touching the edge still counts.
If the operation is "flip a prefix" or "flip a suffix" only one boundary changes, and the answer becomes the number of boundaries instead of half of it.

title: Balance as a walk
when: "Equal numbers of 0s and 1s", "as many a as b", "twice as many"
Bracket sequences: correct, longest correct, minimum changes
Counting substrings by the difference between two counts
idea:
Give one character the score +1 and the other -1 and write down the running total after each position, starting from 0. A substring is balanced exactly when the running totals at its two ends are equal. So counting balanced substrings is counting pairs of equal running totals: sweep once, and for each new total add the number of times it has occurred before.

A correct bracket sequence is the same walk with two extra conditions: it never dips below 0, and it ends at 0. "Longest", "how many changes" and "how many rotations" questions about brackets all become questions about the minimum of this walk.
traps: The total before the first character, 0, must be counted as seen once.
Totals can be negative: use a map, or an array shifted by n.
The answer can be about n squared over 2, so use 64 bits.
For other ratios (say twice as many), choose scores so that a good substring sums to 0: +1 and -2.

title: Palindromes from their centres
when: Count or find palindromic substrings
Longest palindromic substring
"Is the substring from l to r a palindrome?" asked many times
Cutting a string into palindromes
idea:
Every palindrome has a centre, and a string of length n has 2n - 1 of them: n on a letter and n - 1 between two letters. From a centre, grow outward while the two sides match. If the largest palindrome at a centre has radius r, then every smaller radius at that centre is also a palindrome, so the centre contributes r palindromes (counting a single letter as radius 1).

Growing from every centre costs O(n squared) in the worst case, which is fine up to a few thousand letters. For longer strings there is a linear method (Manacher) that reuses the radius of the mirror-image centre inside the largest palindrome found so far, or you can halve on the radius with hashes of the string and of its reverse.
traps: Handle the two kinds of centre separately, or interleave a separator character between the letters so that every palindrome has odd length.
A table is_pal[l][r] filled by increasing length answers "is this substring a palindrome" in O(1), which is what partition problems need.
The count can exceed 32 bits for long strings of one repeated letter.

title: Two answers per subtree
when: Choose vertices or edges of a tree under a rule about neighbours (independent set, cover, matching, colouring)
"Maximum", "minimum" or "number of ways" on a tree
The choice at a vertex restricts only its children and its parent
idea:
Hang the tree from a root. For each vertex keep a small number of answers for its subtree, one for each thing the parent needs to know. For "no two chosen vertices adjacent" two are enough: take[v], the best for the subtree if v is chosen, and skip[v], the best if it is not. Then take[v] = 1 + sum of skip[child], and skip[v] = sum of max(take[child], skip[child]).

The pattern is always the same: decide what the parent has to know about a subtree, make that the index of the table, and combine children one at a time. If the combination depends on how many children are in some state, the combination itself becomes a small knapsack.
traps: Process children before parents: recursion, or a top-down order replayed backwards.
Recursion depth equals the height of the tree; for very deep trees use an explicit order.
Do not walk back to the parent: pass it along, or compare with the stored parent.
For counting versions the values are multiplied instead of added, and need a modulus.

title: Digit by digit
when: Count the numbers up to N (N as large as 10^18) with a property of their digits
"How many numbers in [L, R] ...": answer for R minus answer for L - 1
The property can be checked by reading the digits left to right with a small memory (digit sum, remainder, last digit, whether a digit has appeared)
idea:
Write N in decimal. A number smaller than N agrees with N on some prefix, then has a strictly smaller digit, and after that its digits are completely free. So go through the positions of N; at each position try every digit smaller than N's digit there, and count the ways to fill the remaining free positions so that the property holds, given what the fixed prefix has already contributed. Finally check N itself.

The "free positions" count is a small table: free[k][s] = number of ways to write k digits (leading zeros allowed) with digit sum s. In the general form the table is indexed by (position, summary of the prefix, still tight or not), and a memoised recursion writes itself.
traps: Leading zeros: with a digit-sum property they are harmless, but for properties like "no two equal adjacent digits" you need a "number has started" flag.
Counting from 1 rather than 0: subtract the case of zero if your count includes it.
For a range [L, R] compute f(R) - f(L - 1); do not try to keep two bounds tight at once unless you have to.
The answer can be near 10^18: use 64 bits.

title: Subsets as states
when: n is at most about 20 and something must be assigned, ordered or visited
"Each item used exactly once" with a cost that depends on the pairing or the order
Travelling-salesman-like tours, perfect matchings, covering a small set
idea:
When all that matters about the past is which items have been used, the set of used items is the state. Write it as a number whose bit j says whether item j is used. For an assignment of people to jobs, process the people in order: the number of bits set in the mask tells you whose turn it is, and best[mask] is the cheapest way for the first few people to take exactly the jobs in mask. From a mask, try every job not yet in it.

That is 2^n states with n transitions each, instead of n! orders. When the order of visiting matters as well (a tour), add the last item to the state: best[mask][last], with n squared times 2^n work.
traps: 2^20 states times 20 transitions is about 2 x 10^7: fine. 2^25 is not.
Iterate masks in increasing order: every mask you move to is larger, so its value is final when you reach it.
Shift with 1 << j, and with 1LL << j once n exceeds 30.
Do not store what the mask already tells you: here the person index is the popcount.

title: Intervals as states
when: Neighbouring elements are merged, removed or split, and the cost depends on what is merged
n is a few hundred (cubic time)
Matrix-chain, merging piles, bursting or removing with neighbours, optimal bracketing, palindromes by deleting
idea:
If every operation acts on neighbours, then whatever happens inside a stretch never interacts with the outside until the stretch has become a single thing. So define the answer for every stretch [l, r], and build long stretches from shorter ones by asking: what was the last step inside this stretch? For merging piles, the last step joins a left part [l, k] and a right part [k + 1, r], and costs the total of the whole stretch:

best[l][r] = min over k of best[l][k] + best[k + 1][r], plus sum(l..r).

Fill the table by increasing length. There are about n squared over 2 stretches and up to n split points each: cubic.
traps: Fill by length, not by l then r: a stretch needs all shorter stretches inside it.
Use running totals for the sum of a stretch.
Think about the last operation, not the first: after the first operation the two sides are not independent.
Values grow quickly: n times the total can exceed 32 bits.

title: The prefix function
when: A prefix of a string that is also a suffix (a border)
Find all occurrences of a pattern in a text
The smallest period of a string, or whether it is a repetition of a block
Longest palindromic prefix (on s + # + reverse)
idea:
For each position i, let pi[i] be the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. To compute pi[i], start from k = pi[i - 1], the best border of the previous prefix, and try to extend it by one letter: if s[i] equals s[k], the answer is k + 1. If not, fall back to the next shorter border of the previous prefix, which is pi[k - 1], and try again.

The borders of the whole string are pi[n - 1], then pi of that minus one, and so on: each border of a border is a border. The value k rises by at most one per position and never goes below zero, so all the falling back costs O(n) in total. For pattern matching, compute it on pattern + # + text and look for the value equal to the pattern length.
traps: pi is indexed by position but holds a length: the fallback from length k is pi[k - 1].
Proper prefix: the whole string does not count as its own border.
The smallest period is n - pi[n - 1]; the string is a whole number of blocks only if that divides n.
Use a separator that occurs in neither string when joining pattern and text.

title: Answers for every root
when: "For each vertex of the tree, compute ..." where the answer for one vertex would take a full traversal
Sum of distances from every vertex; farthest vertex from every vertex
A tree DP whose answer depends on which vertex is the root
idea:
Compute the answer for one root with an ordinary bottom-up pass. Then move the root along an edge from a vertex p to its child v and ask how the answer changes. For the sum of distances: the size[v] vertices in the subtree of v each get one step closer, and the other n - size[v] vertices each get one step farther, so

answer[v] = answer[p] - size[v] + (n - size[v]).

A second, top-down pass applies this to every edge. In general each vertex needs the contribution of "everything outside my subtree", which the parent can supply by combining its own outside part with its other children.
traps: Two passes: children before parents, then parents before children.
When the combination is not invertible (a maximum instead of a sum), keep the best two child values or prefix and suffix combinations, so that one child can be left out.
Totals can reach about n squared: 64 bits.

title: Shortest paths with costs 0 and 1
when: A grid or graph where some moves are free and the others cost exactly 1
"Minimum number of walls to break", "minimum number of switches", "minimum number of direction changes"
A shortest-path problem where a priority queue feels like too much
idea: With costs 0 and 1 only, the vertices waiting to be processed always have at most two different tentative distances, d and d + 1. So a double-ended queue can stand in for the priority queue: when an edge of cost 0 improves a neighbour, put the neighbour at the front (it is as near as the current vertex); when an edge of cost 1 improves it, put it at the back. Vertices then leave the front in order of distance, exactly as in the settle-the-nearest method, in linear time.
traps: A cell may enter the deque more than once; only relax when the new distance is strictly smaller.
The cost belongs to the move: here, entering a wall cell costs 1 and entering a free cell costs 0.
For a grid, flatten (row, column) into one index or keep two arrays; avoid a map.

title: A position and a flag
when: "At most one" change, removal, skip or reversal is allowed somewhere in the array
The best answer ending at i depends on one yes-or-no fact about the past
A one-state DP you already know (best stretch, longest run) with one extra permission
idea:
Take the DP you would write without the permission, and make two copies of it: one for "permission not used yet" and one for "permission already used". Every position then has two values, and each is computed from the two values of the position before.

For the best stretch with one removal: keep[i] is the best sum of a stretch ending at i with nothing removed, which is the usual max(a[i], keep[i-1] + a[i]). used[i] is the best sum of a stretch ending at i with one number removed. Either the removed number is a[i] itself, leaving keep[i-1], or it was removed earlier and a[i] is added: used[i-1] + a[i]. The answer is the largest value of either kind.

The second state costs nothing in time. The whole skill is noticing that a yes-or-no fact is all you need to carry.
traps: Write down in words what each of the two values means before writing any transition; most wrong answers come from a vague meaning.
Update order: used[i] needs the old keep, so compute it before overwriting keep.
Empty results: here at least one number must remain, so used does not exist at the first position.
All numbers negative: the answer is the largest single number, not 0.

title: A few stages in order
when: "At most k" actions with k tiny (two trades, three cuts, two disjoint stretches)
The actions must happen in order, and at any moment you are "between" two of them
The straightforward idea needs a loop over where the first action ends
idea:
Name the stages you can be in, in order. For two trades: nothing yet, holding the first share, sold once, holding the second share, sold twice. Keep one number per stage: the most money you can have while being in that stage after the days seen so far. Each new price can only move you from a stage to the next one, so each number is updated from itself and from the stage before it:

hold1 = max(hold1, -p), sold1 = max(sold1, hold1 + p), hold2 = max(hold2, sold1 - p), sold2 = max(sold2, hold2 + p).

One pass, a constant number of states. The same picture handles "split into three parts", "two non-overlapping stretches" and anything else that is a short fixed sequence of phases.
traps: "At most two" comes for free: sold2 is at least sold1 because the second trade can be bought and sold on the same day.
Start the holding stages at minus infinity, not 0: you cannot hold a share before buying one.
If you update the stages in the order above on one day, a share can be bought and sold on the same day. That adds profit 0, so it is harmless here, but check it when the statement forbids it.
With k up to n the same idea becomes a table with k columns; with k tiny, a handful of variables is enough.

title: Two prefixes as the state
when: Two sequences are compared, aligned or merged: common subsequence, edits, interleaving, matching with wildcards
Both lengths are a few thousand (the table has n times m cells)
"The first i items using j of something" is the same shape with one sequence
idea:
The state is a pair: how much of the first string and how much of the second have been dealt with. d[i][j] is the answer for the first i letters of s and the first j letters of t. Look at the last letters. Either they are matched with each other (cost 0 if equal, 1 for a replacement) leaving d[i-1][j-1]; or the last letter of s is deleted, leaving d[i-1][j]; or the last letter of t was inserted, leaving d[i][j-1]. Take the smallest.

The border is the part people forget: turning i letters into nothing takes i deletions, and nothing into j letters takes j insertions. Each row needs only the row above, so two rows of memory are enough.
traps: Fill in d[i][0] = i and d[0][j] = j, not zeros.
Indices: d has (n + 1) by (m + 1) cells, and cell (i, j) looks at letters s[i-1] and t[j-1].
n times m around 10^7 is comfortable; 10^9 is not. With two rows the memory is never the problem.
For the longest common subsequence the same table holds a maximum and the borders are zeros.

title: What the top edge looks like
when: Something is built or tiled row by row, and the board is very narrow (width 2 or 3) but very long
Count the ways, modulo a prime, for n up to a million
Whether a piece can continue into the next row depends on how the previous row ended
idea:
Build the wall from the bottom. After some rows, what matters for the rest is only the shape of the top row: for width 2 it is either one block spanning both columns, or two separate blocks side by side. Call the counts of walls of height i with each kind of top row wide[i] and split[i].

Now add one more row and ask what each kind can turn into. On a wide top: stretch the wide block up, or close it and start a new wide block, or close it and start two separate blocks. On a split top: each of the two blocks is either stretched or closed and replaced, which gives four ways to stay split, or both are closed and a wide block starts. So

wide[i+1] = 2 wide[i] + split[i], split[i+1] = wide[i] + 4 split[i],

starting from wide[1] = split[1] = 1. The answer is their sum. Compute once up to the largest height asked, then answer every query from the table.
traps: Count the transitions by listing them, not by formula: the 2 and the 4 are where everyone slips.
Stretching a block is not the same as closing it and starting an equal one above it: the first is one tall block, the second is two blocks, and they are different walls.
Many queries: precompute to the maximum once, do not recompute per query.
Take the remainder at every step; 4 times a value below 10^9 + 7 already needs 64 bits.

title: Remembering how the string ends
when: Count strings or arrays that avoid a short local pattern: no two equal neighbours, no three in a row, no "ab" followed by "a"
The alphabet is huge (k up to 10^9), so the state cannot name the last letter
Whether the next letter is allowed depends only on the last few letters
idea:
Whether a letter may be appended depends on the end of the string, so the state is a description of the end. The trick is to describe it without naming letters: for "no three in a row" all that matters is whether the last two letters are equal. Let diff be the number of valid strings whose last two letters differ (or that have length 1), and same the number whose last two are equal.

Append a letter. A different letter from the last one can always be appended, in k - 1 ways, and lands in diff. The same letter as the last one can be appended only to a string in diff, in one way, and lands in same. So

diff becomes (diff + same)(k - 1), same becomes the old diff.

Because the letters are interchangeable, two states stand in for what would otherwise be k squared of them.
traps: Both new values use the old ones: update them together.
k is up to 10^9: reduce it modulo the prime before multiplying, and note k - 1 can be 0.
Length 1 belongs to diff with count k; same starts at 0.
If the forbidden pattern names particular letters, the letters are no longer interchangeable and the state must say more.

title: Longest increasing subsequence
when: The longest increasing (or non-decreasing) subsequence itself, with n too large for the quadratic DP
Fewest removals to make an array sorted; fewest decreasing sequences needed to cover an array
Pairs or boxes that must nest: sort by one coordinate, then this on the other
idea:
The quadratic DP asks, for each i, for the best earlier j with a smaller value. Turn it round: for each length, remember the smallest value that an increasing subsequence of that length can end with. Call it tail[len]. Two facts make this fast. First, tail is itself increasing, because a subsequence of length len + 1 contains one of length len ending lower. Second, a new number x changes exactly one entry: it extends the longest subsequence whose tail is below x, so it replaces the first tail that is not below x (or is appended at the end).

So each number costs one binary search. The length of tail at the end is the answer. The contents of tail are not an actual subsequence, only the best endings.
traps: Strictly increasing: replace the first tail >= x (lower_bound). Non-decreasing: replace the first tail > x (upper_bound). Mixing them up is the classic mistake.
To print the subsequence, store for each element the position it took and the element before it.
Longest decreasing: negate the values or reverse the array.
For pairs sorted by the first coordinate, break ties by the second coordinate in the opposite order, so that equal firsts cannot chain.

title: Each item at most once
when: Choose some of n items under a capacity, each item used at most once
n times capacity is around 10^7 or less
"Can these numbers be split into two equal halves", "which totals are reachable" are the same table with true/false
idea:
best[w] is the largest value that fits in capacity w using the items looked at so far. A new item of weight wt and value v offers one more option for every capacity: best[w - wt] + v. The only subtlety is the order in which the capacities are updated. Going downward from the full capacity, best[w - wt] has not been touched yet in this round, so it still describes the world without the new item: the item is used at most once. Going upward, best[w - wt] may already include the item, and it gets used again and again, which is the other knapsack.

One array, n times W steps.
traps: Downward loop for each-item-once; upward for unlimited copies. This is the whole difference between the two.
Stop the loop at w = wt; below that the item does not fit.
Values add up beyond 32 bits.
If the capacity is huge but the values are small, swap roles: smallest weight for each total value.

title: Tables on a graph without cycles
when: Longest path, number of paths, or best score in a directed graph that has no cycles
Dependencies: "this must come before that", and you want the longest chain
Any DP whose states do not come in an obvious left-to-right order
idea:
A DP is always a walk over a graph without cycles: states are vertices, transitions are edges. When the graph is given to you directly, the only new question is the order of evaluation, because the labels of the vertices say nothing. Take a topological order: one in which every edge goes from earlier to later. Then process the vertices in that order and push each value along its outgoing edges: longest[b] = max(longest[b], longest[a] + 1).

The order comes from repeatedly removing a vertex with no incoming edges left (a queue and an array of in-degrees). The other way is a recursive function with memory, which is the same computation, but on a path of 200000 vertices the recursion is too deep.
traps: Do not assume edges go from a smaller label to a larger one.
A vertex is finished only when all its incoming edges have been processed; that is exactly what the in-degree count guarantees.
Counting paths: the same loop with a sum, taken modulo the prime.
If the graph has cycles, shortest-path style reasoning is needed and this does not apply.

title: Expected values, from the end
when: "Expected number of steps / rolls / moves until ..." with an answer modulo a prime
A random process that only moves forward
Probabilities given as fractions that you must not turn into floating point
idea:
Let E[i] be the expected number of further rolls when standing on square i. One roll is made for certain, and then you are on one of k squares with equal chance, so

E[i] = 1 + (E[i+1] + ... + E[i+k]) / k, and E[i] = 0 once i is at the end or beyond.

The unknown on the left depends only on squares further on, so fill the table from the end backwards. This is the general rule for expected values: define the expectation of what is still to come, and go backwards. (Probabilities of having reached a state go forwards.) The sum of k consecutive values is a window: keep running totals from the end so that each square costs constant time. Dividing by k modulo a prime means multiplying by the inverse of k.
traps: Answer "as a fraction modulo p": do every division with a modular inverse, and compute the inverse of k once.
Squares beyond the end count as 0; cap the window at n instead of making the array longer.
Subtracting running totals modulo p can go negative: add p back.
If a move can leave you where you are, E[i] appears on both sides; solve that equation for E[i] by hand first.

title: Sums over all subsets of every mask
when: For every mask you need something over all its submasks (or all its supermasks)
Counting pairs with a AND b = 0, or a OR b = something, for values below 2^20
The obvious loop over submasks of every mask is 3^n and n is about 20
idea:
Think of a mask as a point with n coordinates, each 0 or 1. "Sum over all submasks" is a prefix sum in n dimensions. A two-dimensional prefix sum can be made by summing along rows first and then along columns; in the same way, sum along one bit at a time. For bit b, every mask that has the bit adds the value of the same mask without it:

for each bit b: for each mask containing b: f[mask] += f[mask without b].

After bit b has been processed, f[mask] holds the sum over all masks that agree with it above bit b and are submasks of it on bits 0..b. After all bits, it is the sum over all submasks. That is n times 2^n additions instead of 3^n.
traps: The bit loop is the outer loop. With the loops the other way round, values get counted many times.
Supermasks: the same with "mask does not contain b" and adding f[mask with b].
To undo it (from subset sums back to the original values), run the same loops with subtraction.
Sums of 2^n values overflow 32 bits quickly.

title: A transition that is a range sum
when: Counting DP where the new value is a sum of a whole stretch of old values
The honest transition costs O(k) per cell and that is one factor too slow
Each child / day / slot takes "between 0 and a_i" of something
idea:
ways[j] is the number of ways to hand out j sweets among the children seen so far. The next child, with limit a, takes some amount t from 0 to a, so

new[j] = ways[j] + ways[j-1] + ... + ways[j-a].

That is a sum of consecutive entries of the old row. Build the running totals of the old row once, and every new entry is one subtraction. The table costs n times k instead of n times k times a. Whenever a transition reads a contiguous range of the previous row, the same trick applies; when it takes a minimum of a range instead, the tool is a sliding-window minimum.
traps: The range is cut off at 0: the lower end is max(0, j - a).
Subtraction modulo the prime can go negative.
Build the running totals from the old row, not from the one being written.
Start with ways[0] = 1: there is one way to give nobody nothing.

title: A recurrence taken 10^18 steps
when: A DP with a handful of states and the same transition at every step
n is up to 10^18, so even one pass is impossible
Fibonacci-like recurrences, counting walks of a given length in a small graph, tilings of a narrow strip
idea:
When every step of a DP computes the new states as fixed sums of multiples of the old ones, a step is a multiplication of the state vector by a matrix. For "never three in a row" the states are (diff, same) and one step is

diff' = (k-1) diff + (k-1) same, same' = diff,

so the matrix has rows (k-1, k-1) and (1, 0). Doing n - 1 steps is multiplying by the matrix to the power n - 1, and a power is found by repeated squaring exactly as for numbers: about 60 squarings for 10^18. With s states each multiplication costs s cubed.

The work is all in the first part: writing the DP so that the step does not depend on the position.
traps: Count the steps carefully: length 1 is the starting vector, so the power is n - 1, not n.
Matrix multiplication is not commutative; be consistent about whether vectors are columns or rows.
Reduce k modulo the prime before putting it in the matrix; products of two residues need 64 bits.
A constant term in the recurrence is handled by adding a state that is always 1.

title: Every palindrome in linear time
when: The longest palindromic substring, or the number of palindromic substrings, with n in the hundreds of thousands
Queries "is s[l..r] a palindrome" (hashing also works)
Expanding around every centre is quadratic on strings like aaaa...a
idea:
For each centre, store the radius of the longest palindrome around it. Expanding from scratch at every centre is slow only when palindromes are long and overlap, and that is exactly when earlier work can be reused. Keep the palindrome found so far that reaches furthest to the right, say it covers [l, r]. A new centre i inside it has a mirror image j = l + r - i on the other side of that palindrome's centre, and everything around j that stays inside [l, r] is copied around i. So start the radius at i from min(radius[j], r - i) instead of from zero, then expand by comparing letters as usual.

Every successful comparison after that start pushes r to the right, and r only ever moves right, so the total work is linear. To treat even and odd lengths together, put a separator between all letters (a#b#a): then every palindrome has a centre on a position.
traps: The copied radius must be cut at the border r: beyond it nothing is known.
With separators, a radius in the padded string equals a length in the original; decide the conversion once and test it on "aa" and "aba".
Update l and r only when the new palindrome reaches further right.
Number of palindromic substrings: each centre contributes one per possible radius.

title: Merge the smaller into the larger
when: For every vertex of a tree, something about the set of values in its subtree (distinct colours, most frequent colour)
Sets or maps are merged again and again, and you fear it is quadratic
Components are united and each one carries a collection
idea:
Give every vertex the set of colours in its subtree. A parent's set is the union of its children's sets plus its own colour. Copying sets upward is quadratic on a path. Instead, the parent takes over the largest child's set as it is (a swap, no copying) and inserts the elements of the other, smaller sets into it one by one.

Why this is fast: follow one element. Each time it is moved, it lands in a set at least twice as large as the one it left. A set cannot hold more than n elements, so an element is moved at most log n times. All moves together: n log n insertions.
traps: Always insert the smaller into the larger; compare sizes and swap first.
Take the big set over by swapping or by keeping an index to it, never by copying.
Record the answer for a vertex right after its merges; the set is about to be swallowed by the parent.
On a path of 200000 vertices recursion may overflow the stack: process vertices in reverse breadth-first order.

title: Sweep a line, keep what it touches
when: Geometry with axis-parallel segments or rectangles: count crossings, area of a union, points inside rectangles
Two coordinates, and a condition on both
Offline queries that can be sorted by one coordinate
idea:
Move a vertical line from left to right. At any moment the line touches some horizontal segments; keep the heights of exactly those in a structure. A horizontal segment enters the structure at its left end and leaves at its right end. When the line reaches a vertical segment at x, the horizontals it crosses are the ones currently in the structure with height between its lower and upper end: a range count.

So: turn everything into events sorted by x, and use a Fenwick tree over the heights (compressed, since they go up to 10^9) for "add 1 at y", "remove 1 at y" and "how many in [y1, y2]". One dimension has become time, and the other a data structure. That sentence is the whole technique.
traps: Ties at the same x need an order. If touching counts: insert first, then query, then remove.
Compress the coordinates that index the tree.
The count can be about n squared over 4: 64 bits.
The structure holds only what the line touches now; forgetting to remove is the usual bug.

title: Meet in the middle
when: n is about 40: too many for 2^n, far too few for anything polynomial to be the point
Choose a subset to hit a target sum, with values too large for a table over sums
A search of depth d where 2^d is too much but 2^(d/2) is fine
idea:
Split the numbers into two halves of 20. Each half has only about a million subsets, so list all subset sums of each half. A subset of the whole is one subset of the left half together with one of the right half, and its sum is the target exactly when the right sum equals the target minus the left sum. So for every left sum, count how many right sums equal what is missing: sort the right list and binary search, or sort both and walk two pointers.

2^40 has become 2^20 times a logarithm. The pattern is general: enumerate each half completely, then combine the halves with sorting or a lookup instead of trying all pairs.
traps: Count equal sums with multiplicity: use the range of equal elements (upper bound minus lower bound), not a yes-or-no search.
Build the list of sums by doubling (each new number adds a shifted copy), not by looping over bits for every mask.
The answer can be as large as 2^40: 64 bits.
A hash map with a million keys is slow and easy to attack; sorted arrays are safer.

title: A stretch is a pair of prefixes
when: Count the stretches (subarrays) whose sum is a given value, is divisible by k, or has some property of the sum
Count substrings with equally many of two letters, or with an even count of every letter
"Number of subarrays such that ..." with n too large for trying every pair of ends
idea:
The sum of a stretch is the difference of two running totals: sum(l..r) = P[r] - P[l-1]. So a condition on a stretch is a condition on a pair of running totals, and counting stretches is counting pairs. The sum is divisible by k exactly when the two running totals leave the same remainder modulo k. Walk through the array keeping a count of how many earlier running totals had each remainder; at each position, add the count for the current remainder to the answer, then record the current one.

The same sentence solves a whole family: sum equal to x (look up P - x), equal numbers of two letters (count +1 and -1), even counts of every letter (the running total is a bitmask and the operation is xor).
traps: The empty prefix counts: start with the remainder 0 already recorded once.
Negative numbers: in C++ the % of a negative number is negative; bring it back into 0..k-1.
Look up first, then record the current prefix, or a stretch of length zero gets counted.
The number of stretches is about n squared over 2: 64 bits.

title: Printing the answer, not just its size
when: "Print the length, and then one such sequence / path / set" after an optimisation that a table solves
Any DP where the judge wants the actual choices: the subsequence, the items in the knapsack, the route
"If there are several answers, print any"
idea:
The table of best values already contains the answer; it only has to be read back. Stand on the cell that holds the final value and ask which transition produced it: the cell says "I am 1 more than the diagonal cell because the letters match" or "I am equal to the cell below" or "I am equal to the cell to the right". Follow that transition and repeat until you fall off the table.

Filling the table from the far ends towards the start (so that len[i][j] speaks about the two endings) lets you read the answer back from the front, in the right order, with no reversing. The other common way is to fill forwards and store in each cell where its value came from, then walk back from the end and reverse.
traps: The whole table must be kept: the two-row memory trick destroys what the walk needs.
Compare with the same rule the table was filled with; when two neighbours tie, either may be followed.
Filling forwards means walking backwards: the result comes out reversed.
Any valid answer is accepted by a checker, so your output need not match the sample; but the length must be optimal.
